title: A woman of valor (Proverbs 31:10–31)
hookLine: many homes sing Eshet Chayil on Friday night to honor the women of the house

lines: THE ONE WHO KEEPS IT RUNNING.
SAID OUT LOUD, IN FRONT OF EVERYONE.
cards: Somebody in your life keeps everything running and almost never hears about it. They know where the birth certificates are, remember everyone's allergies, and fix the thing before anyone notices it's broken.

When did someone last say, out loud, in front of everybody, what they do? In many Jewish homes on Friday night, someone at the table does exactly that, in a song whose words come straight from the Bible.

teach.b: It's the last chapter of the book of Proverbs, and it opens, in the old Jewish Publication Society translation: "A woman of valour who can find? For her price is far above rubies." Eshet is woman.
Chayil is a strong word: strength, ability, even an army. Valor is a good translation. This isn't a delicate portrait.

teach.h: A FIELD, A VINEYARD, AN OPEN HAND.
teach.b: The woman in the poem buys a field, plants a vineyard, runs a business, stays up late, gets up before dawn, feeds her household, opens her hand to the poor, and speaks with wisdom and kindness.
"Strength and dignity are her clothing," it says.
The poem is an acrostic: its twenty-two verses begin with the twenty-two letters of the Hebrew alphabet in order, alef to tav, as if to say, praise her with every letter there is.
In many homes it's sung on Friday night, often by a husband to his wife, sometimes by the whole family.

The Kabbalists who made it part of the Friday night table also read it about Shabbat itself, or about God's presence, the Shekhinah, and some read it about the Torah. Jews read it in different ways today.
Some sing it to wives and mothers, some to every woman at the table. Some feel its ideal is a heavy one to live up to, and choose other readings, or sing it to honor someone they've lost.
The book of Ruth calls Ruth a woman of valor too, with the same Hebrew words.

teach.h: LET HER WORKS PRAISE HER IN THE GATES.
teach.b: And the poem ends with public praise: "let her works praise her in the gates." Don't keep it private. Say it where people can hear.

how: In many homes, Eshet Chayil (Proverbs 31:10–31) is sung at the Friday night table before Kiddush, often by a husband to his wife or by the whole family.

o: a quiet, obedient wife who stays at home
a woman who fought as a soldier in Israel
a woman of strength, praised in Proverbs

games.q: what's inside the poem — tap the pairs.

s: the woman in the poem stays quietly at home
she buys a field, plants a vineyard, runs a business and opens her hand to the poor.
the poem is an alphabet acrostic
its twenty-two verses begin with the Hebrew letters in order.
Ruth is also called a woman of valor
the book of Ruth uses the same Hebrew words about her.

games.q: the poem has praised the woman's work all the way through. in its last line, where does it say her praise belongs?
games.why: "let her works praise her in the gates": the city gate, where people gathered. praise said where others can hear.

practice: Picture someone you live with, or someone you love who's far away, and walk through their week the way the poem walks through hers: what did they carry, and what did they do that nobody thanked them for?
Pick one specific thing, not a general compliment, and shape it into one clear sentence you could say where they can hear it, maybe where others can too.

wordCard.voice: Eshet chayil, Hebrew for a woman of valor: the poem that ends Proverbs, sung on Friday night to praise the strength of a woman's work.

orig.note: Hebrew: a woman of valor. chayil also means strength, wealth, or an army.

carryVoice: Your line: say the praise. Alef to tav, every letter of it. Day one hundred four, done.
